title: Answers kept apart
hookLine: this year each tradition answers in its own voice, and we don't blend them into one

lines: A RULE BEFORE THE FIRST ANSWER.
cards: Squeeze every tube in a child's paint box onto one plate and stir. Red, blue, yellow, the lovely violet. What you get is brown.
Each color was beautiful on its own; stirred together, they cancel each other out.
Wisdom from many traditions can go the same way: a little from here, a little from there, stirred into one soft answer that nobody actually holds. This year we'll hear a great many answers.
So first, a rule for how we hear them.

teach.h: A BLENDED ANSWER BELONGS TO NOBODY.
teach.b: First, a blended answer belongs to nobody. Take suffering. The Buddha names craving as where it comes from.
Job, in the ashes, argues his case before God. Stir those into everything happens for a reason, and you've lost both. So every answer this year is named: the Buddha's is the Buddha's, Job's is Job's.

teach.h: EACH ANSWER COMES WITH A LIFE.
teach.b: Second, each answer comes with a life. A teaching isn't a loose sentence floating in the air. It lives inside practices, a community, a long line of people who read it and argued about it.
To hear it well, hear where it lives.
Third, alike is not the same. Some lines do sound close. Soon we'll hear the Dhammapada say that hatred ceases by love, and later in the year Jesus will say, love your enemies.

They can sit side by side as neighbors, but one belongs to the Buddha's sayings, the other to the Sermon on the Mount, and each makes the most sense in its own house. So notice the echo, and leave each line at home.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.
teach.b: The letter of James puts it plainly: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath."
And from a very different house, the old biographer Diogenes Laertius reports the Stoic Zeno saying that we have two ears and one mouth so that we might listen more and talk less.
Two houses, two sayings, each in its own words, and neither needs the other to make its point. Together they set this year's rule: hear the answer out before you reply.

how: Some interfaith study groups let each tradition speak in its own texts and terms, and ask members of that tradition to explain it, rather than merging teachings into one shared answer.

games.q: two lines from two traditions sound almost the same: hatred ceases by love, and love your enemies. what does this year do with them?
o: decide which one says it better
notice the echo, and leave each line in its own house
games.why: neighbors, not one teaching: the Dhammapada's line belongs among the Buddha's sayings there, Jesus's to the Sermon on the Mount.

practice: Listen to the room for a moment, picking out one sound, then another, without calling them good or bad.

Then make yourself a small promise for the year, in your own words: when a tradition answers one of the six questions, you'll hear it out to the end before you agree, disagree or mix it with anything else.
